explanation: A snake's lower jaw is split at the chin and joined by stretchy tissue, so each side spreads and moves on its own. Nothing comes out of joint.

claims.text: Snakes do not dislocate their jaws when swallowing large prey.
The left and right sides of a snake's lower jaw are not fused at the chin but are joined by elastic tissue.
Each side of a snake's lower jaw can spread and move independently, which lets the snake swallow large prey.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Wide gape without dislocation: The Natural History Museum explains that large-prey snakes don't unhinge or dislocate their jaws to eat – their mouths are just really stretchy. The lower jaw's two halves are linked by a ligament, and each half connects to the skull through a mobile joint, which lets the sides spread apart.

claimResults.note: The summary names the Natural History Museum page 'Snakes: Super senses, stretchy jaws and deadly venom' (Tier B) for this sentence; peer-reviewed PMC papers in the same list confirm the unfused mandibular symphysis. A first call (W1, counted here, query 'do snakes actually dislocate their jaws to swallow prey, lower jaw halves joined by ligament') also confirmed the claim through the NHM, Scientific American and Smithsonian, but its summary flagged a National Geographic general snake page that still says the lower jaws 'unhinge'. That is the myth itself, yet the summary reported it as a conflicting source, so W1 is not used here. Myth screen: confirmed with web evidence in this check.

evidence.restatement: A snake's two lower-jaw bones are not fused at the chin; a stretchy ligament joins them.
